items.text: Poland began two days of national mourning Sunday, and police said the three people found dead at the Kraków gunman's home were his parents and sister.
items.detail: The 24-year-old suspect, who authorities say held far-right, ultranationalist views, is in critical condition in a hospital after police shot him during Saturday's attack, which killed six people and wounded 15 in the Old Town's Main Square. The family home is in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Kraków, where police said several firearms were seized; he and his father belonged to a shooting club. A British national was among the dead, and the wounded include citizens of Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia. Two police officers who stopped the attacker are hospitalized, one in critical condition. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called it far-right terrorism; the square stayed partly sealed off Sunday.
items.why: Officials are treating Poland's rare mass shooting as terrorism as the country takes stock of the dead.

items.text: Saudi Aramco's tower in Riyadh was damaged by falling debris Sunday after Saudi air defenses intercepted missiles fired at the capital by Yemen's Houthis.
items.detail: The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed two ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh and later two cruise missiles and a drone over the Riyadh and southern regions; another missile aimed at the Eastern Province was also intercepted. Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry called it an attempted attack on an Aramco administrative building and said shrapnel caused limited damage and no injuries; witnesses saw blown-out windows across several floors of the tower in the King Abdullah Financial District. Civil Defense alerts in Riyadh and other cities were lifted after the danger passed. The Houthis had not claimed the attack. It follows Saturday's airstrikes near Sanaa that the Houthi-run health ministry blamed on Saudi Arabia. Separately, the United Arab Emirates said it rescued 22 crew members after a fire broke out aboard a cargo ship in the Sea of Oman.
items.why: The renewed Saudi-Houthi fighting is now reaching the Saudi capital and the state oil company at the center of world oil supply.

items.text: Iran hanged three men Sunday over January's anti-government protests in Karaj, its judiciary said, accusing them of armed unrest and working for Israel and the U.S.
items.detail: The judiciary named the men as Hassan Divband (rendered Dioband by Reuters), Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh and said they used firearms, grenades and Molotov cocktails, set fire to public facilities and damaged an electricity substation, causing power outages. The Supreme Court upheld their death sentences and their assets were ordered confiscated; eight co-defendants received prison terms of five to 10 years. Rights groups have said protest cases relied on rushed trials and coerced confessions.
items.why: The executions extend Iran's wave of hangings tied to the January uprising.

items.text: A gunman killed six people and wounded at least 15 in Kraków's Main Market Square on Saturday; Poland's defense minister called it an act of terror.
items.detail: Police said the 25-year-old Polish suspect drove to several spots around the square in Kraków's Old Town shortly after 3 p.m. local time and opened fire with an automatic weapon at each stop before officers shot and wounded him; he is hospitalized after surgery. Four women and two men were killed; police said at least one victim was British. Two police officers were among the wounded. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect was fascinated by far-right ideologies and held "ultranationalistic" views, and that he may have taken the weapons from his family's home, where his father held gun permits. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Saturday evening that two women and a man were found dead in the suspect's home and were likely close family members. Authorities said there is no indication of a second attacker.
items.why: It is one of the deadliest mass shootings in modern Polish history, in the heart of a major European tourist city.

items.text: President Trump said he is ordering the Justice Department to investigate Democratic leaders over what he called threats against Republicans.
items.detail: In a Truth Social post Saturday, Trump said Democrats were "threatening a lot of people, including the Attorney General," with impeachment and other punishment, called it "extortion at the highest level" and wrote, "I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!" He did not identify the "threatening letters" he cited, who sent them or who received them, and gave no evidence of a crime. He singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan. The White House and Slotkin did not immediately comment, and the Justice Department has not announced an investigation.
items.why: It comes days after Democrats won both chambers and are signaling oversight of the administration.

items.text: The U.S. military disabled a cargo ship trying to break the Iran blockade and set up a new task force to choke Iran's land and Caspian routes.
items.detail: U.S. Central Command said a U.S. aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of the St. Kitts-flagged M/V Huda in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday after its crew ignored repeated warnings and tried to leave the region following a call at an Iranian port; the crew had been told to leave the targeted spaces. CENTCOM said blockade enforcement since July has redirected 147 vessels and disabled five that refused to comply. Separately, CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper ordered the formation of Task Force Iron Gate, a staff of about 20 civilian and military personnel in Tampa that will work with other agencies to stop weapons, dual-use technology, sanctioned goods and illicit revenue from moving across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea. CENTCOM estimates the naval blockade has kept Iran from exporting more than $25 billion in crude oil. Also Saturday, Iran's Revolutionary Guard spokesman said the country had lifted its self-imposed 2,000-kilometer limit on missile range.
items.why: Washington is widening its pressure on Iran from the sea to land routes as fears of a renewed war rise.

items.text: Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main challenger, will get the first chance to form Israel's next government, President Isaac Herzog announced Saturday.
items.detail: Herzog informed Eisenkot and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of his decision Saturday evening and will formally hand Eisenkot the mandate at a ceremony Sunday. Eisenkot, a former military chief who leads the Yashar party, was recommended by parties representing 67 lawmakers, against 46 for Netanyahu. He has 28 days to build a coalition of at least 61 of the Knesset's 120 seats, with a possible 14-day extension. His four-party bloc won 48 seats in the Oct. 27 election and Netanyahu's bloc 53. Earlier Saturday, Netanyahu called for a national unity government.
items.why: It is the closest Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, has come to losing power since 2021.

items.text: The Justice Department is joining Texas' $1.8 billion Medicaid-fraud lawsuit against Planned Parenthood, according to a court filing.
items.detail: The department said in a filing late Friday that it intends to intervene in the 2021 False Claims Act case in federal court in Amarillo, brought by outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and an anonymous whistleblower. The suit says Planned Parenthood kept billing Texas and Louisiana Medicaid after the states moved to cut it off and did not repay the money once the terminations took effect; the plaintiffs seek about $1.8 billion in repayments and penalties. Planned Parenthood says the billing was legal while courts had paused the terminations, has said a loss would force it to shut down in Texas, and said Saturday it will fight the case at trial, expected in 2027. The Justice Department under President Biden declined to join the case in 2021. The filing came days after Texans elected Democrat Nathan Johnson as the next attorney general.
items.why: Federal backing raises the stakes in a case Planned Parenthood says could close its Texas clinics.
items.source: U.S. District Court, N.D. Texas (docket) / Reuters

week.text: Congress will be controlled by Democrats in January after they won both the House and the Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections, AP projected.
week.detail: AP called the Senate for Democrats late Tuesday and the House early Wednesday. Democrats flipped at least seven Republican-held Senate seats: Kansas (Adam Hamilton over Sen. Roger Marshall, the state's first Democratic senator since 1932), Iowa (Josh Turek over Rep. Ashley Hinson), Texas (James Talarico over Ken Paxton), Ohio (Sherrod Brown over Sen. Jon Husted), Maine (Troy Jackson over Sen. Susan Collins), North Carolina (Roy Cooper) and South Carolina (Annie Andrews). They held Georgia (Sen. Jon Ossoff), Michigan (Abdul El-Sayed) and New Hampshire (Chris Pappas). In the House they flipped more than two dozen districts. As of 4 a.m. Eastern, Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi were still uncalled. Hakeem Jeffries is in line to become the first Black House speaker. Trump wrote that he "wasn't on the Ballot," vowed to veto Democratic bills and told Fox News he would accept the results; Senate Majority Leader John Thune vowed to resist the new majority's agenda. The new Congress is sworn in in January.
week.why: Democratic majorities can block Trump's legislation, reject his nominees in the Senate and open investigations of his administration for the last two years of his term.

week.text: Stephen Miller will become White House chief of staff on Monday, replacing Susie Wiles after Republicans lost Congress.
week.detail: President Trump said Friday that Miller, the deputy chief of staff for policy and a longtime immigration hardliner, takes over Nov. 9. Wiles, the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff, submitted her resignation Thursday night and will move to the Trump Political Operation. The change comes after Democrats won both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's midterms.
week.why: It is the top White House staff change after the midterm defeat.

week.text: U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October and the unemployment rate edged to 4.1%, the Labor Department reported.
week.detail: Nonfarm payrolls rose 165,000, well above the 48,000 average monthly gain over the prior 12 months. The unemployment rate changed little at 4.1% from 4.2% in September. August was revised up by 53,000 to +186,000 and September up by 31,000 to +60,000, a combined +84,000. Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% to $38.00, up 3.1% over the year. Gains were led by professional and business services (+70,000), health care (+42,000) and transportation and warehousing (+25,000); manufacturing added 19,000. People working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million.
week.why: The main monthly jobs gauge came in much stronger than the recent trend, three days after the midterms.
